Paver Sealing & Restoration · Kissimmee, FL

Paver Sealing and Restoration in Kissimmee

Cleaning, re-sanding and sealing pavers in Kissimmee costs $1.50–$3.25 per sq ft (clean, re-sand, seal), a Florida market range as of October 2026. Toho Water Authority's twice-a-week schedule governs irrigation, not a hose-fed pressure washer, so cleaning pavers ahead of a seal doesn't have to wait for a particular day of the week.

A pre-seal pressure wash doesn't follow Toho's watering calendar

Toho Water Authority, the city's own utility, runs a year-round schedule: odd and no-number addresses water Wednesday and Saturday, even addresses water Thursday and Sunday, with nothing allowed between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. (Toho Water Authority, Watering Days and Times). That calendar covers sprinklers and irrigation heads watering grass, and a hose running through a pressure washer to blast algae and dirt off a paver surface simply isn't the same category of water use, so the clean-and-re-sand step before sealing books around the crew's schedule and the forecast rather than a numbered address day.

Dry sand or polymeric sand: two different joint materials

Plain dry sand gets swept into the joints and compacted, but it stays loose and can migrate out again over time, especially where water moves through regularly. Polymeric sand works differently: it's swept in dry the same way, then lightly misted with water, which activates a binder that locks it in place and resists washout far better than plain sand does. Neither is required by the paver industry's own guidance, so the choice on a Kissimmee job comes down to how much resistance to washout is worth paying for upfront.

Resealing a Kissimmee paver driveway, worked out in square feet

Say a 480 square foot paver driveway gets a full clean, a polymeric re-sand and a seal. Pricing that at $1.50–$3.25 per sq ft (clean, re-sand, seal) puts the job around $720 to $1,560, with releveling any sunken pavers pushing it toward the higher figure. On a rental-zoned property with weekly guest turnover, that same job often gets scheduled on a shorter cycle than an owner-occupied driveway would need, since the joint sand and surface wear faster under steady vehicle and foot traffic.

Rental-zoned patios and driveways see joint sand wear out faster

On lots zoned for short-term rental use, where a driveway or paver patio sees a new set of feet and vehicles every few days, joint sand washes out and pavers settle unevenly faster than on a lot with one household's ordinary traffic (Osceola County, STRPD District). Re-sanding with polymeric sand before sealing holds up better under that turnover pace than standard sand does, which is one reason property managers on those lots often schedule sealing more often than a homeowner on an inland, owner-occupied street.

Sealing joint sand before it's had time to compact

Sand swept into the joints right before a sealer coat goes on, without a proper compaction pass first, ends up trapped loose under a hardened surface rather than locked in place the way it should be. That weakens the very interlock the joint sand is meant to provide, and it can show up months later as pavers that shift slightly under traffic even though the surface looks sealed and finished. A Kissimmee job that rushes straight from re-sanding to sealing without pausing to compact is cutting a step that doesn't show its cost until later.

How joint sand loss and base erosion feed each other

Joint sand isn't structural, but it does one real job: keeping water from reaching the base directly through the gaps between pavers. Once sand washes thin in a joint, more water gets through to the aggregate below with each storm, and that accelerated erosion is part of why the same joints keep losing sand faster once they start. Re-sanding protects the base indirectly by closing that path, which is why it's paired with cleaning and sealing rather than treated as a separate service on a Kissimmee paver surface.

Washing at an angle instead of straight down into the joints

A pressure washer aimed straight down into a joint strips out whatever sand is left there, which defeats the point of a cleaning pass meant to prep the surface for fresh sand, not empty it further. Crews working a Kissimmee job wash at an angle across the paver field, keeping the wand moving rather than dwelling on one spot, and save the direct, close-range pressure for stains that genuinely need it. That distinction between cleaning the surface and accidentally re-opening every joint is one of the easiest steps to get wrong on a rushed job.

Keeping grit off a sealed surface between full cleanings

A light sweep and the occasional rinse between professional sealing visits keeps windblown sand and grit from scratching the sealer coat underfoot, since that fine abrasion is a slower but steadier wear factor than any single storm or cleaning. A Kissimmee patio near an unpaved area or a driveway that collects blown sand from a neighboring lot benefits more from this habit than a surface set well back from loose ground, simply because there's more grit arriving on it in the first place.

Frequently asked questions

Is a city or county permit required to reseal a Kissimmee paver driveway?

Neither office treats maintenance on pavers that are already down as something to review. The slab and driveway permits both offices use are built around new construction or expanding a paved area, not around washing, re-sanding or sealing a surface that's already in place.

Can pavers be pressure-washed on a day Toho Water Authority doesn't allow irrigation?

Yes, since the irrigation schedule has nothing to do with a pressure washer. A sprinkler head watering grass and a hose feeding a pressure washer aren't regulated the same way, so the pre-seal rinse can happen any day a crew and the weather line up.

How often should pavers on a rental property be resealed?

More often than an owner-occupied driveway typically needs, since steady guest turnover wears joint sand and surface sealer down faster. There's no fixed interval set by any code; it depends on how much traffic the surface actually sees between sealing jobs.
